Almost every one of the witnesses, managers of the mills, and in some instances, owners of the mills, were in a large majority of cases strongly in favour of exclusion and considered that there was an abundance of Chinese for all purposes in the province. The wages paid to white labour in Washington state are higher than they are in British Columbia. The general evidence given by the managers of the lumber industry was that there was an abundance of Chinese, that if no more Chinese or Japs were allowed in the country the industry would suffer no loss or even inconvenience, but on the other hand it would be a great benefit to the country. All agreed that this class of immigrants was undesirable as citizens, and all expressed strong opinions favourable to higher restriction. On the Amerieau side Chinese labour is not employed in this industry, and the American mill owners are strongly in favour of their present exclusion law.
The canning industry of British Columbia is as important as any of the great industries in the province. The number of Japanese and Chinese engaged in it greatly exceeds the number of them employed in any other industry. According to the evidence, more than one half of the labour employed in the canneries is Chinese labour ; in fact the canning process is almost entirely in the hands of the Chinese, and although the canners' evidence in some cases was strongly in favour of Chinese labour in this industry, it was admitted that the present supply already in the province was quite sufficient to meet all requirements and supply all demands for years to come ; and it is considered that the change by the process of only prohibiting Chinese from coming into the province, while such large numbers are already here, will make the change so gradual as to be all but imperceptible.
On the Sound where the Exclusion Act is applied it has not retarded the development of this industry.
If the present condition of things continues in this industry in British Columbia, it will not be long before the whole business of the country will be in the hands of a dozen exploiters and gangs of Chinese and Japanese.
It has been well established that the general industries referred to will not be interfered with by any exclusion law, the present supply being abundant for all purposes and for years to come ; this fact being well established beyond doubt by the employers themselves, and I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that even the employers of the province, whose position generally is one of taking every advantage of cheap labour have stated beyond doubt that it is desirable to restrict the inflow of Chinese and Japanese labour. The permanent settlers of that province are face to face with a serious effect upon two important factors of citizen-Mr. SMITH (Vancouver).
ship, namely, the unskilled labourer and the youth of the' country. These are the people who ought to be encouraged to come to the country, but very many, both skilled and unskilled labourers, with women and children, already in the province and very many who have come to the province to seek employment have found the usual opportunities for it, especially in the lower grades of labour, already absorbed by Chinese and Japanese. Very many skilled workmen going to British Columbia find no opening in their trade. Being willing to take any position, these, with the larger class who have no special calling or trade, are debarred from almost every leading industry in the province, unless they are willing to compete at wages acceptable to Chinese and Japanese. In the city of Victoria alone there are 63S Chinese labourers, in Vancouvir City there are 220 Chinese labourers, and by the evidence given by men in a position to know it is clearly proven that whilst there are many unskilled workmen in the cities, almost every avenue of work of this kind is already filled by Chinese or Japs. This evidence is beyond question as proving also the serious position that we have to face with regard to the employment of boys, girls and women, the occupations of this class being all taken up-by the Chinese. This is especially important as it relates to the boys. I state on the floor of this parliament to-day that there are hundreds of boys, practically young men, who ought to be taking up the different kinds of labour in the province and thus assist their parents who are not in a position to keep them idle, who are completely shut out and wandering the streets without an aim or a purpose, because the Chinese are employed in the avocations rightly belonging to them. Thus the youth, the future hope of the country-are developing the character of idleness, and in every instance large numbers of them are going over into the United States. Very many have left British Columbia and have already gone there ; in fact I believe we are supplying that country on the other side, so far as* the west is concerned, with the very best of our youthful labour and thus depleting our own country. I insist that this aspect of the question, depleting as it does this country of its future citizens, is a most serious grievance which ought to be at once rectified. As a matter of fact the employment of Chinese in all these grades of manual labour deters the youth from seeking employment because of the Chinese being employed at this work.
The Chinese monopolize entirely the position of domestic servants. It is considered by those who employ them in their homes that this is one of the instances where the Chinese are a great benefit to the country, and where it is repeatedly stated that it is impossible to get white females. We forget, however, that by the constant use and appropriation of Chinese labour in this business

we are making the proper training of domestic servants of tlie female subjects of tlie country an impossibility. There are plenty of girls in British Columbia at liberty to work as domestic servants, but they have no encouragement, they have to compete against the regular, docile, slavish, condescending methods of the Chinese domestic. He is willing to be there at all times, to do all things, to meet all exactions, to answer every demand. He is not a servant, he is a slave. Thus, the daughters of citizens of the country, have to compete against this kind of thing. Many have tried to do it, but the people generally have got so well used to the Chinese domestic-the poor slave who answers every call, meets every demand-that it is an impossibility for the free, ambitious white female domestic to meet these demands. Thus we are closing up what ought to be a school of training for females of the country. We are shutting them out from their natural avocation and they wander the streets in idleness whilst the Chinaman occupies the home.
Look at the case of merchant tailors. The evidence given by the report of the commission proves conclusively that whilst the Chinese labour monopolizes the menial and unskilled employments, in some instances they have very dangerously encroached upon the different trades and callings where higher wages are paid. In the city of Victoria the tailoring business has almost entirely been handed over to the Chinese. In 1891 there were eighteen white tailor shops and 150 men and women employed, with a yearly wage of over $109,000, at an average weekly wage of from $18 for men and $10 for women. In 1900 there were only twenty-one white men and thirty women in the whole tailoring business of the city of Victoria, and the yearly wages were $22,000 as against $109,000 ten years previously. In the same decade the population of the city had doubled.
One witness who was a high class tailor and has carried on the business for many years says that the wages of the white tailor in that city have been reduced fifty per cent through Chinese competition, that he had been driven almost entirely out of the business.
The same thing is true of the Wholesale manufacture of clothing. This work of course is done principally by women and Chinese. This again has been taken almost entirely out of the hands of the whites by the Chinese. One firm who put in a plant costing $2,000 with the latest machinery, employed over forty hands, and the Chinese killed the business completely. Every one of the employers In this business agreed that the present supply of Chinese was ample and that no injury would follow if the Chinese were entirely excluded.
The same thing holds good with regard to other trades and callings-the boot and shoe manufacture, the cigar making, the brick
making, lime burning, eordwood cutting, railway construction, freighting ; all these have been taken charge of by the Chinese, and all these are avenues of labour which very properly belong to the white labour of the country, labour which means permanence and stability to the country itself. In this again, let me add, the operations of any of these industries, according to the evidence given by interested persons, will not be even inconvenienced by the exclusion of the Chinese. In every instance in connection with every trade and every business the one conclusion is proved that the present supply of Chinese and Japanese in the province of British Columbia is quite sufficient to meet the demands of the business. The one argument in the past-it has been put up by Chinese advocates, an argument of course which the government lias had to pay some regard to-has been that the industrial development of the province made Chinese immigration to the province absolutely necessary. If the truth of that position is admitted for the sake of argument, the time has come, as I have just said when all companies with large investments and interests, and all their managers responsible for the most economic results that their business can bring, the principal business men in all the cities, with their large investments, unitedly agree at the present time that there is a superabundauee^of Chinese and Japanese in the province. The argument then in favour of entire exclusion is absolutely conclusive.
The merchants and the traders in the province are unanimous in favour of Chinese exclusion, and I would recommend the House to read the Commission's Report from page 610 to page 624 ; every one of the witnesses, the leading business men in tile Coast cities, are unanimously in favour of entire exclusion. In Victoria, according to the figures of the Chinese Board of Trade itself, there are 238 Chinese merchants, comprising 109 firms, and doing a business amounting to over a million dollars. In 1 an-couver there are 143 merchants, comprising forty-seven firms, doing a business of over one half a million dollars. At Nanaimo there are fourteen merchants, doing a yearly business of $163,000. At New Westminster there are twenty-nine Chinese merchants, doing a business of $317,000. And amongst the whole of the whites, merchants and traders, according to the evidence, they are unanimously opposed to the Chinese.
The question then is:	Are the people
of British Columbia or is the public opinion of that province, favourable to further restriction or entire exclusion of the Chinese? The important question is : Do the persons representing all classes of business interests in the province, favour further restriction or exclusion ? For the present, I am shutting out of the argument bona fide employees, for the sake of avoiding commonly I accepted opinion that this agitation for

Chinese exclusion relates entirely to the trades unionists of the province. This class, I may say, whose evidence X consider is of as great an importance as others, 1 leave out of the present consideration for the reason that both skilled and unskilled labourers in the province are absolutely unanimous in favour of entire exclusion. But when I speak of the opinions of the others. I mean professional men, traders of . every description; the largest employers of labour-the most of whom employ already in some degree Chinese and Japanese labour. What is the general opinion of these people, as the whole of their interests are at stake with regard to this question. Now, Sir, I have looked over the whole of that evidence, and there we have the heads of the principal dry goods merchants, the heads of the principal grocery merchants the head of the legal firms, the superintendents of the large coal mines, the superintendents of the metalliferous mines, the principal ministers of the principal churches, the manar-gers of the lumber business, the representative men, and every conceivable interest in the province. Their evidence is there under oath, and almost unanimously they agree with the entire exclusion of the Chinese. If this request is not granted by this parliament, then the desire of the people of British Columbia is not answered. What good reason can any government give, what good reason can any parliament give, composed as it is, of the representatives of the people, for refusing to grant the people their desires ?
Similar agitations have been made on tli's self-same question in other countries, and what British Columbia is asking for and has been demanding for many years has been already accomplished and acquired 4n other countries. It is well known, and important for this House to consider, that in other countries where Chinese have efiii-grated to that their presence and exclusion has been agitated for very strongly. That is seen in the United States, Australia and Tasmania. As far back as 1876, a Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Representatives was appointed to investigate the question of Chinese emigration, and I think it important that quotations from the report of that commission might be given to show that exactly a similar experience with our own was proven. The testimony of lawyers and of doctors, merchants, divines, judges, in fact of all classes, went to prove that there was no real prosperity derived from the presence of the Chinese, that they were ruinous to the industrious labouring classes, that they promoted a caste, that they were dangerous to free institutions, that they reduced wages to starvation point, that they made unskilled employments impossible, that they compelled young men to grow up in idleness, that the whole tendency was to turn industrial classes into an almost entirely servile class.

They found that the Chinese could subsist where the Americans would starve; they dispensed entirely with what was a necessity in modern civilization; to compete with them, said the American commission, is to drive out every American subject. It was also proven that the very presence of Chinese retarded white immigration to the Pacific States. This arose from the Chinese monopoly of farm and mechanical work, and the low price of their labour, which made it impossible for the new immigrant to live. This commission declared that free institutions, founded on free schools and intelligence, could only be maintained when based on intelligent and adequately paid labour; that adequate wages are necessary to give self-respect to the labourer and the means of education to liis children; for family life is the great safeguard to political institutions. That Chinese immigration meant sordid wages, no public schools and the absence of the family; and they reported to Congress that this problem was too important to be treated with indifference, but that it was absolutely necessary to solve the difficulty unless their Pacific possessions were to be given over to an alien, race. And in their concluding statements to congress they said it was the part of wisdom to anticipate the day when patience might cease, and that wise legislation ought to avert this evil, that impending difficulties of this character should not in this advanced age be left to the chance arbitrament of force, that these questions ought to be solved by the statesman and philanthropist, and not by the soldier. And the committee concluded its report by stating that in view of the fact that the well-known policy of the Chinese government is adverse to the immigration of its citizens, and that Great Britain has already, without offence to China, absolutely prohibited immigration to several of her colonies, we believe that similar action-on our part will not destroy or disturb the friendly conditions now existing; but even if it were otherwise the harmony and perpetuity of our social and political institutions cannot be weighed in the same balance with mere material prosperity or commercial advancement. Your committee, therefore, unanimously recommend that immediate correspondence be opened up with the governments of China and Great Britain.
In 1879, a Restriction Act was passed in the United States, "being vetoed by the President in the same year. A treaty, however,,, was entered into in 18S0, ratified and proclaimed in 1881, between the United States and China, as to the exclusion of Chinese coming into the States. This, of course, especially provided for the immigration of Chinese labourers, and protecting as it did the Chinese already permen-ently residing in the States.
In 1882, an Act was passed giving effect to this treaty. In 1881 this Act was amended, suspending the immigration of Chinese

into tlie States for ten years, and imposing a penalty of $500, or a term of imprisonment for one year for every Chinese labourer brought in by the master of any vessel. In 1892 a further Act was passed, continuing the operation of all restrictive laws then in force for a period of ten years, and making provision at the same time for deportations for breach of law.
This treaty was the result of nearly twenty years of agitation. It is also to be noticed that by a Joint Resolution of the House, July 7, 1898, it was declared that there should be no further immigration of Chinese into the Hawaiian islands, except upon the conditions allowed by the law of the United States. These acts and treaties, with the regulations to enforce the same, constitute the present law of the United States with respect to Chinese immigration.
In the report of the Philippine commission in 1900, (volume 2, page 432), there is a memorandum of the Chinese in the Philippines, and coming from such a trustworthy source it is worthy of special notice. Their report was : That the principle of political economy is well known, which lays down the rule that in order for a country to obtain advantages from immigration the immigration should bring in capital, new industries or superior knowledge to perfect industries already in existence, or at least that such immigrants should apply their energies to pursuits productive of gain, not only to the immigrants themselves, but to society in general in the country in which they have established themselves, or that they finally become assimilated with the people of the country, thus giving, although indirectly, stimulus to certain professions and industries whose progress is a consequence of the increase of the numbth- of inhabitants of the town. Chinese said they, in going to the Philippines did not comply with any of the conditions of this well-known condition of political economy, which are desirable points to be looked for in immigrants. Why should they be allowed to emigrate to the Philippines when their presence was not a guarantee of prosperity and progress for the rest of the inhabitants. It is impossible, they said, on account of the competition in which they lived to attain a position in the middle class of society. It was the custom of the Chinese to consume, as far as the necessaries of life are concerned, food, clothing, and articles which they import from their own country for their own purpose.
The report of the Canadian Royal Commission has made extensive inquiry into the application of the exclusion principle in the United States, has taken most important evidence in Seattle, in Washington state, in Portland and in San Francisco, and there we have evidence of a most important kind, having had so many years' experience with this class of people in the western States, and also considerable experience with the application of an Exclusion Act, brought about by treaty between the governments of the United States and China. The general effect of this restrictive legislation in the United States has been to gradually decrease the number of Chinese on the west coast, the greatest reduction, of course, taking place in California, where they were reduced from 72,000 in 1890, to 45,000 in 1900. The population of the State of Washington has increased from 75,000 in 1880, to 518.000 in 1900, while the number of Chinese have only increased from 3,186 in 1880, to 3,629 in 1900; while the population of British Columbia has increased from 49.459 in 1880, to 177,272 in 1900; the Chinese population for that same period in British Columbia has increased from 4,550, to 10.000; so that whilst the increase in the general population of British Columbia has doubled, the Chinese population has more than trebled. In Seattle they have a population of 80,000, and they have less than 500 Chinamen; whilst in Victoria., the capital city of British Columbia, with a population of only 20,000, they have a Chinese population of 3,300.
The whole of the evidence taken in the western States was overwhelmingly in favour of the present operation of the exclusion Jaw in the United States. This opinion was given principally by employers of labour. They stated plainly that the exclusion caused no shock to the various industries; the change was gradual; the effect was unnoticed. And in the western States, as proven by the evidence given to our Royal Commission, it was clear that they regarded the question as being closed, and it could not be found that there was any class of the populace but were in favour of Chinese exclusion. The consideration of the continuation of that treaty between the United States and China is being dealt with at the present time. Special reference was made to the importance of the subject by President Roosevelt in his annual address, and when he declared emphatically his anxiety for a continuation of the exclusive measures, and there was every evidence that that would be carried out according to the present discussion on the question.
The Australian colonies prior to the formation of their present commonwealth, had passed restrictive legislation against the Chinese. The colony of Victoria as far back as 1855 imposed a tax of $50 and limited the number to one Chinaman to every ten tons of the ship's burthen, and imposed a penalty on the master of the vessel of $50 for every passenger carried in excess. They imposed a resident license tax on the Chinese of $20. In 1881 the same colony passed an Act limiting the number of Chinamen to one in every 100 tons of th >
ship's burthen, and imposing a penalty of $500 for breach of the law and a tax of $50 for every immigrant arriving in the vessel. Similar legislation to this has been passed

easy. One tiling is wanted and that is population, and not the quantity of immigrants, but in every case the suitability of them. I am not sure that the nature of the immigrant brought in under the present emigration policy of the government is at all desirable. One thing is sure, whether he is suitable cr otherwise, he is costly. If this parliament concludes in favour of Chinese and Japanese by refusing to exclude them, I do not see any reason that they can give for not throwing the gates wide open and admitting them as freely, not only as they would be willing to come, but making inducements for them to do so. If the decision of this parliament is in favour of Chinese immigration then the logical meaning of that ought to be that the enormous expense of the present immigration policy of the government in settling up the country is altogether unjustifiable when we have countless numbers of Chinese willing to come in without any expense at all to the country. That seems to me to be the logical position that this parliament ought to take, if it holds the view that entire exclusion against Chinamen is wrong. If we are to have a strong nation we must have a united people, thus the nature of the immigrant must be such as to make an affiliation possible with the present Canadians.
This does not exist at the present time in British Columbia. AVe are mixed up with large proportions of a servile race, and whatever permanently weakens British Columbia, weakens the Dominion, and weakens the empire, and any method of business operation which brings material gain to individual interests ought not to weigh for one moment against an injury to the nation.
Then as to the moral aspect of the question. I know it will be said by certain people that this question is opposed to the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. The morality of Chinese exclusion is not to be compared to the morality of international warfare. AVe do not propose to organize a system of slaughter agaiust the Chinamen ; we do not even propose to expel those from our country who are already in it ; we have been and are quite ready to bestow on them the benefits of British institutions ; we are content at least to adopt nature's method of lessening the evil effects of a class of people by the ordinary process of natural destruction. AVe do not propose to send our armies to China ; we simply request them to stop at home. Honourable gentlemen who would sanction and endorse considerations readily in favour of international material warfare I suppose would hold up their hands in holy horror against the proposed legislation that we advocate. It is beyond the possibility of proof by those who oppose such legislation that it is possible to raise the Chinaman up to the appreciation of the moral and Christian people of this country or even to make him a good citizen. If that were possible to any Mr. SMITH (Vancouver).
conceivable extent it might be urged perhaps from a humanitarian standpoint that it would be our duty to receive them ; but as I look over the evidence of the late commission I find that the prominent Christian teachers in the province of British Columbia clearly show that it is not possible to make go d citizens of the Chinese or in any perceptible degree to bring them under the influence of Christian teaching. I know In some cases where Christian teachers living in the east have held the contrary view, who have afterwards lived in the west and have changed their views. This is especially true to the politician of every grade. AVbilst it lias been difficult to have this legislation endorsed enthusiastically in this parliament, especially by the members of eastern Canada, it is not difficult and has never been difficult to get a favourable opinion from any cf them when they are out in the west. I desire, therefore, to read some of the evidence of the leading ministers of the Christian churches in British Columbia.
It will be seen, by looking over that evidence and admitted by Christian teachers, that missionary work amongst the Chinese on the coast has met with little success, in fact where any of the ministers gave evidence at all favourable to the Chinese it was put on the ground that they were a servile class and that such a class was necessary to the higher development of the Anglo-Saxon race.
The Rev. AA7. Leslie Clay minister of the principal Presbyterian church in Victoria, who has lived there for seven years, states as follows : That where any single Chinese gives evidence of Christian reformation he is looked upon by his fellow Chinamen with great antipathy ; he is east oft' by his friends because of having adopted Christian modes of thought and living. That he does not know of any of the educated classes of Chinese accepting Christianity. The presence of them in large numbers, he says, is not desirable, and states emphatically that he objects to more coming in. AA7e should have a strong robust nation, he said, and our vast resources ought to be developed by our own citizens. He was asked the question on what ground would he exclude any part of God's creatures from any part of the world, and he answered that self-preservation was the first law of nature, that he would exclude them on that principle and that the Imperial government ought to make a treaty with China to that effect. They were a servile race. Asked as to what he thought the founder of the Christian religion would advise under the circumstances, he answered and said that he had endeavoured to interpret Christ's mind in the matter, and thought that Christ would approve of selfprotection.

Rowe, minister of the Metropolitan church, of Victoria, formerly of Toronto, considered that the presence of Chinese had a detrimental effect on the pro-

vince and an injurious effect upon white labour and on the markets. Their presence is a decided injury to economic conditions, and altogether a disadvantage to the community. The Chinamen are driving the white men out of the country. The Chinaman can never be made a citizen, and that is what we want, people that will take an interest in our laws and institutions and be an integral part of our community and not a menace to the community. He said he believed entirely, not in restriction, but in prohibition, speaking from a national standpoint. He thought Canada would be much stronger by the exclusion of the Chinese race.
Bishop Perrin, head of the Anglican Church, says : They come without a cent and are under obligation to those who bring them here. I do not think, he says, that things ought to be allowed, to go on as in the past. They are allowed to come in and arrive with nothing. I think our mission is to go to China because our religion is the universal religion. He thought the Chinese ought not to be allowed to interfere with the dignity of labour in the mind of a true ideal workman. He was opposed to the present immigration. Encroachment of Chinese on the occupations of the people of the country was a dangerous and objectionable condition. I may state, he said,-and this is a very important point-that, while I was in England I was unwilling to recommend labouring people to come to British Columbia. I thiuk there is a great future for British Columbia when the population increases.

Hall, Chinese missionary of the Presbyterian church, says : There are large numbers of Chinese employed in and about the Union Mines. When a Chinaman becomes a Christian he is ostracised, shut out from his family, cut off from all intercourse, is made an outcast of his own race. We have no converts from amongst the merchant class. I do not favour the formation of a coolie class at all.
The Rev. Mr. Scott, Methodist minister, the First Methodist church, Vancouver :-
I do not think it desirable to have the Chinese come. They do not assimilate. It would not he desirable if they did. I have no ill-will to those who are here, but I wouldn't permit any more to come. I think their presence unnecessary. I do not think we need them1 here in order to reach the Chinese nation as a whole, from the Christian standpoint. We can take Christianity to China without their presence heTe.
Tbe question was asked, ' Do you believe in the universal brotherhood of man ?' ' I do,' he said, ' and I believe in the common Fatherhood of God.' And would you deny the right of any man to any portion of this earth ? ' He answered :
We are not universal nations yet; universal nationality and universal brotherhood are two different things. We would like to see universal Christianity, but that is still in the distant 51
future. I don't expect to live to see any great approach towards the universal brotherhood of man. When the Chinese come to the province by the thousands affecting the industrial work of the labourer then the first duty is for the national government to protect its own people and send the aliens back to their own land.
The Rev. McBeth, Presbyterian minister, Vancouver : Any alien race which refuses to assimilate is a menace to the nation. ' I think,' he said, ' we have all the Chinese we can digest. Looking at this question we must have regard for the future of the country. Our children must have room for livelihood. Domestic servants are held in low esteem in British Columbia on account of the presence of Chinese.'
The Rev. John Reid, Presbyterian church, believes the Chinese ought to be excluded.
The Rev. Roland Grant, Baptist minister, ten years on the coast, was also in America for years-had had large experience with Chinese, said :-Assimilation with other nationalities is forbidden. In Portland, he said, with a population of 20,000, in 1880, Chinese population was 6,000. Since the application of exclusion of Chinese, Portland has a population of 100,000 and only 5,000 Chinese. I think we have the moral right to exclude. I think the operation of the Exclusion Act would be quiet and unobserved. The Chinese coming to. this country as they do have a deteriorating tendency. A tax of $100 will not keep them out. The Exclusion Act is the proper thing.
The Rev. Mr. Bowell, Methodist minister : I consider the immigration of Chinese and Japanese to be detrimental to the interests of the country. They control the work that ought to be in the hands of white people. Many people have left the province, large families, not being able to get work. I regard them as a menace to the future wellbeing of the nation, and very seriously interfere with the employment of the boys, which is a very serious matter for any country.
The Rev. Mr. Minchester, Toronto ; The presence of Chinese in British Columbia in some cases affect the white wage-earners favourably; in others prejudicially. If Chinese were coming into the country in large numbers I would favour restriction, not of Chinese alone, but I would restrict the large influx of foreigners from any quarter. I would base terms of restriction upon character and education. Foreign immigrants should be able to read some European language, should come into the country for some stated purpose should show some reasonable prospect of becoming permanent citizens.
The evidence then of a large majority of the witnesses under this head goes to prove that, the opinions of the leading Christian ministers in British Columbia who understand the question, who know its effects, who are in a position to know all the facts



relating to It, unite with those of others in the province in favour of the exclusion of Chinese. The opinion is practically unanimous that the work of Curistianizing the Chinamen in the country is not attended with as satisfactory results as similar work in their own country. The great majority of these witnesses were positively opposed to a servile class or to the introduction in any way of a class that would tend to degrade or affect the welfare of the white labouring class. It is therefore clearly proven and reported so by the commissioners that in no appreciable measure will the missionary work with the Chinese as a nation be affected, and that the morality of this question is supported even by the leading Christian teachers in the province where the evil exists.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am drawing to a conclusion on this subject, and I desire to make a recapitulation of my points in order that they may be thoroughly clear to the mind of the House. I gave first a description of the quality of the report of that commission, which must be admitted by the House as being extensive and conclusive. Second, I presented the demands of British Columbia on this question, showing that for fifteen years the agitation has been going on, the unanimous voice of the provincial parliament by the passing of. legislation of every description and resolutions and unanimous petitioning of the people. Third, I reviewed the work of the Dominion government on this question from 1884 up to the present time. Fourth, I described the scope of the inquiry and the finding of the commission, and proved conclusively that what the people of British Columbia had been demanding for many years had been demonstrated by the conclusion of the commissioners to be reasonable. Fifth, I showed how the Chinese affected the different industries: (a) how they affected the question of land clearing and land settlement, (b) how they affected the coal mining industry, (c) how they affected the lumber industry, (d) how they affected the fishing and canning industry. Sixth, I showed how the Chinese excluded unskilled labourers and displaced the boys, the great mass of British subjects, heads of families depending upon the operation of unskilled industries for a livelihood, but more especially the boys of the country, the future nation, driven to idleness, ought to be assisting the sustenance of their family, deprived of the ordinary employments of the province. Seventh, I showed how they affected the local industries; how local industries of many kinds had been entirely taken possession of by them, and how the whites had been driven out of the business altogether, as instanced by the merchant tailors, boot and shoe manufacturers, cigar makers, brickmaking, cordwood cutting, railway construction, freighting, and that in all the evidence given that the business would not

be inconvenienced by Chinese exclusion. Eighth, I showed the opinion of the people of British Columbia-public opinion on the question; I demonstrated clearly that the evidence of every interest in the country, dry goods merchants, grocery merchants, lawyers and barristers, superintendents of large coal mines, superintendents of metalliferous mines, ministers of Christian churches, managers of the lumber business, representative men of every interest, were agreed for greater restriction and even exclusion. Ninth, I showed the agitation of the question in other countries, as seen in the United States, in Australia and Tasmania for many years back, how they accomplished and operated what we are now demanding; then the findings of our own commissioners, the unanimous decision in favour of an immediate increased restriction. and failing a prohibitive treaty, the law of exclusion. Tenth, I made some reference to the trade relations with China, showed the experience of the United States, operation of the Exclusion Act in that country had not in any way interfered with the trade, but on the other hand their trade connections had increased enormously. Then I looked at the moral aspect of the question, and by the production of evidence given under oath, by the leading! ministers of the Christian churches of British Columbia, they were almost unanimous in favour of a prohibitive law, and very strongly in favour of an increased exclusion law.
I do not see how this parliament can refuse to at once comply with the wishes of the loyal and industrious subjects of British Columbia, and as the representative of that province, in complete accord with the opinion of the witnesses in the evidence given to the commission, and with the conclusion arrived at by the unanimous commissioners, I hope that this parliament at this session will take such immediate action as will comply with the requests of the people of British Columbia, and remove this grievance once and for all. I can assure this House that the feeling of British Columbia subjects on this question is intense, and whilst they have appreciated the increased head tax of 1900, and especially appreciated the appointment of the Royal Commission, , and now that they find that the decision of that commission is entirely in accord with their experience and with their desire, it would be a most serious matter if this parliament does not immediately comply with their unanimous request.

I have listened attentively to the speech which the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) has just delivered upon the question of the exclusion of Chinese from British Columbia. I have tried to follow him closely, and I think I express the opinions of a

good many members on this side of the House when I say that we believe he has done his duty, and that he has made a very temperate as well as a very forcible presentation of the case from the standpoint of the province of which he is one of the representatives. I agree with him too, Sir, speaking for myself, and I concur in his opinion that he cannot see, in view of the report which the Royal Commission appointed by this government has made on that question, and in view of the unanimity of feeling which exists amongst the people of that province, how parliament can very much longer refuse to deal summarily and finally with this matter. I may remind my hon. friend that he has still another string to his bow. I think, if my memory serves me right, that immediately prior to the elections of 1896 the attention of the right hon. the First Minister was called to this question of Chinese immigration. His opinion on that matter was asked by some of his friends on the Pacific coast. I would not like to make any statement that was not in accordance with the facts, but I believe I am correct in saying that in response to the message which the right hon. gentleman received from his supporters in British Columbia on that occasion, he said that he would be guided by the opinions of Ills friends and supporters in that province .in the action which he would take on that question if the Liberal party "were returned to power. He has a number of able and loyal supporters from that province, and they have made a presentation of the case to him again and again. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat has made an exhaustive and elaborate presentation of the case, and I would invite him now at the earliest moment to test the sincerity of his leader upon the question of the exclusion of Chihese from the province, by giving notice of a resolution to that effect, and having a vote of this parliament taken upon it.
I was much gratified to notice that the Minister of Labour was present during the whole time that my hon. friend was addressing the House. He has taken a good deal of interest on this question of protecting the rights of labour. I am sure that my hon. friend from Vancouver must have convinced him" by the arguments which he has so temperately and so forcibly advanced to-day. I have no doubt that if the suggestion which I have taken the liberty of making to the hon. member for Vancouver is acted upon, and if he gives the House an opportunity of expressing its opinion on this matter, he may look for the cordial co-operation and support of the hon. Minister of Labour. At any rate, if the hon. member for Vancouver will do what I think he ought to do, implement his speech by action, if he will present to the House a resolution calling for the exclusion of the 51*
Chinese, he may be able to test the sincerity of hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House and ascertain where they stand upon that question.
The hon. gentleman also made reference to the quality of our immigration, which I think is worthy of the very best consideration of hon. members on both sides of the House. He did not confine his remarks to Oriental immigration, he referred to other classes of immigration coming to this country from the east. I agree with him that quality in our immigration should not be overlooked, that we should endeavour to get the very best class of immigrants to come to Canada, and that the presence of undesirable classes, not only in British Columbia but in other provinces of the Dominion, acts as a deterrent to prevent the better classes that we desire to come to the Dominion, from entering our doors. I took the liberty already, during this session, of drawing the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, and I think of the Minister of Finance, to the allegations which were made in the annual report of the Commissioner of Immigration of the United States, as to the difficulty which the authorities on the other side of the line experience in keeping undesirable immigrants out of that country. In view of the fact that the hon. member for Vancouver has referred to the quality of immigration, I take the liberty again of drawing the attention of the governnfent to the statements which the Commissioner General of Immigration for the United States has made in his report for the fiscal year ending June, 1901. After referring to the number of diseased immigrants who were returned by the officers of his department from United States ports to the countries whence they had come, he says :
These represent, however, only such as- applied for admission to the United States, and the bureau reiterates the opinion heretofore expressed that the vigilant Inspection at our ports has resulted, to some extent, in diverting diseased aliens to Canada, whence they surreptitiously effect an entrance across our northern boundary line.
Now, Sir, in view of this statement of the hon. member for Vancouver, concerning the desirability of having none but the best class of immigrants coming to Canada, I think the extract I have read is worthy of the attention of the government, and I think they should direct their efforts to keeping out of our country this objectionable class, that, according to the report of the commissioner, is seeking entrance to the United States by way of Canada. I hope that the speech which has been made by the hon. member for Vancouver will have some effect upon the government, that it will stir up the Minister of Labour, that" it will induce him to take some such steps as will meet with the reasonable demarids which have been presented to the House by the hon. member for Vancouver.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some passing reference to an incident which is not, probably, unparalleled in the history of this House, but which is unique in its character, nevertheless, which took place during the sitting of this House yesterday. I refer to the extraordinary opinion which hon. gentlemen who occupy seats in this House entertain respecting each other; I refer to the extraordinary spectacle, if I may use that strong language, presented to the House and to the country yesterday by the hon. gentleman who represents North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) in this House, and by his colleague who sits beside him, the hon. gentleman who represents the county of Russell (Mr. Edwards). The confession, if I may be permitted to use the term, which the hon. member for North Norfolk made, was certainly a most extraordinary one. I think it was well that even at this late date that confession should have been made, and I am glad that the hon. gentleman had the courage to make it. It is a most extraordinary one in its character. The hon. gentleman stated briefly to the House yesterday that he was a protectionist-a protectionist to the hilt-while his colleague at his right (Mr. Edwards) says he is a free trader to the hilt. The hon. member for North Norfolk declared that not only is he a protectionist now, but that he has been a protectionist steadily for the past twenty-five years and that he believes in moderate protection : that in 1875, 1876, and in 1877, he advised his leaders that the country required moderate protection and that the great bulk of the people of Canada were looking for legislation of that character. That statement was made by the hon. member for North Norfolk, if I understood what he said correctly in the House yesterday. He said that he had advised the government of the late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie that additional duties should be imposed in order that the interests of the country might be protected, and having made this statement, he made the still further and most extraordinary statement that the late Mr. Mackenzie and his colleagues were prepared to give the industries of this country an additional measure of protection and that the reason why they did not give that protection was because they met with so much opposition from their supporters from the maritime provinces. That, I believe, was, in brief, the statement which the hon. member made. Lest I should have misinterpreted what he said, with the permission of the House, I will read the ' Hansard ' report of that particular part of his speech :
I suspect, however, and I think I have good reason'; for the suspicion-that the Mackenzie government were willing to advance the duties to 20 per cent or even to 221 per cent. But, the Minister of Finance of that day-
I think the Minister of Finance of that day is the veteran parliamentarian who occu-

pies the position of Minister of Trade and Commerce to-day.

But the E'inance Ministrr of that day was
waited upon by a delegation of the members from the maritime provinces headed by the Hon. A. G. Jones, then member for Halifax, and was informed by that delegation that if any advance in the duties was made it simply meant that there would be a bolt of the supporters of the government from the maritime provinces.
So that, the honest convictions of the hon. member for North Norfolk and of the Liberal government of that day were set aside. The interests of the country were set aside. Patriotism on their part was set aside also in order that by acceding to the demands [DOT] of the gentlemen who then represented the maritime provinces in this House, the Liberal party might secure a renewal of power from the electorate when the appeal was made in the summer of 1878. That seems to be the position in which the hon. member for North Norfolk has left his colleagues respecting their action in refusing the moderate demands of the country as far back as 1878 for a reasonable measure of protection to the industries of Canada. The hon. member for North Norfolk goes a little further and says :
I wrote, as I say, to the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie in June 1878	I advised him
to postpone the date of the elections and to take measures to have this question thoroughly discussed in every riding in the Dominion and to have this protective policy combated by good speakers 'everywhere.
The hon. gentleman, who was in favour of the principle of moderate protection for the industries of Canada, this gentleman who thought that the interests of the country would be promoted by the adoption of a reasonable measure of protection, this gentleman who asked his leader, the late Mr. Mackenzie, to give that measure of protection, this gentleman who says that he believes that Mr. Mackenzie and his colleagues were in favour of giving a measure of protection to the industries of Canada and that the request was refused because the Liberal representatives from the maritime provinces figuratively put a pistol to the head of the government, says that he wrote to the late Hon. Mr. Mackenzie asking him to postpone the elections in order that a competent band of speakers might be sent out to convince the electors of Canada that the protection that he believed to be in their interest should not be granted them. I think this is a most extraordinary statement for an hon. gentleman to make. We are bound under the rules of parliament, and we unhesitatingly acquiesce in them, to accept that statement ; but, I say that coming from an hon. gentleman occupying such an honourable and distinguished position as that hon. gentleman occupies in this House and in this country, it is one of the most extraordinary character for him to make. But, fortunately, or unfortunately,
the hon. gentleman's statement can be buttressed by a statement made by an even more distinguished member of this House than himself, the statement of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads this House. He practically endorses the statement made by the hon. member for North Norfolk in sentiments which fell from his lips at the banquet which was given in the restaurant of the Senate to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce . (Sir Richard Cartwright) in May, 1900. If I have copied correctly from the Toronto ' Globe ' of May 10th of that year, the utterances which are credited to the right hon. gentleman, he said on that occasion that :
When the policy of the party was agreed upon Sir Richard Cartwright never wavered in his support of it .	. In the days of Mr. Mackenzie,
when the country was much depressed, there were many who believed that if the tariff was increased that policy would be justified by the necessities of the revenue, and that it would be a valuable policy for the iountry .at large	 but if the advice of Sir Richard had prevailed at that time this policy would have been adopted. If it was not accepted it was on account of other influences, which prevailed with the government of the day, and for 16 or 20 years Sir Richard bore the brunt of the obloquy of not having responded to public sentiment, whereas the truth was he was ready to respond to public sentiment.
That statement, it seems to me, confirms the statement which the hon. member for North Norfolk made respecting the action of the government of the late Mr. Mackenzie in dealing with the trade issues of this country. 1 say it with the greatest possible respect, it is a most extraordinary statement to have been made by the hon. gentleman who represents North Norfolk, but it seems to be confirmed by the statement which the right hon. leader of the government made at the banquet to which I have made reference. Patriotism and the interests of the country, so far as one may judge, were sacrificed on that occasion by hon. gentlemen opposite in the hope-the vain hope-that they might secure a renewal of office from the electors of this country. The hon. member for North Norfolk says that he was fully aware of the strength of the public opinion which existed in the country at that time, that he himself took time by the forelock, that he addressed many meetings in his own constituency against this very principle of protection in order that he might retain his seat in this House. We have the spectacle presented to us of an hon. gentleman who believed in the policy of protection from 1878 down to 1896, denouncing that policy and declaring against the legislation, brought in by the late Sir John Macdonald and the Conservative party, known as the national policy, which, he asserted, yesterday, in this House, was moderate in its character, was moderate protection, was
protection in the 'interests of the people of this country. Is not that a most extraordinary spectacle for an hon. gentleman to present ? Is it not an extraordinary position for one to take who occupies the position that the hon. member for North Norfolk occupies in the House aud in this country ? What an inspiration it will be to the young men of Canada to be told by the hon. member for North Norfolk that while he believed in moderate protection-and he tells us now that the legislation passed by the Conservative party was of this class, that it was moderate protection-that while he believed in that policy, that while he believed that a moderate measure of protection was necessary to promote the interests of the country, yet from 1878 down to 1896 he did not hesitate to condemn the policy of Sir John Macdonald, he did not hesitate to fulminate against protection and use his great power and influence throughout the Dominion to induce the people of Canada to desert the standard of Sir John Macdonald and give their support to himself and his colleagues.
Sir, the memory of Alexander Mackenzie is revered by the people of this country. There is a well known maxim which tells us : Speak nothing but good of the dead. I regret that the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) who was associated for years with Mr. Mackenzie in public life, who on many occasions expressed himself as favourable to the Mackenzie government, should be one of the first in this House to asperse the memory of Mr. Mackenzie. Colleagues of the late Alexander Mackenzie, who are equally responsible with that gentleman for the legislation of 1876, have now seats on the floor of this House, and some of them seats in the present administration. The hon. Alexander Mackenzie has passed over to the majority; he has entered into rest; he has gone to his reward, but bis colleagues are here in the House to face the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) and, if he has vials of wrath to pour, it is on their heads he should pour them, and not on the head of the deceased statesman who cannot defend himself. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) before attacking the motives which prompted Mr. Mackenzie to decline to give that reasonable measure of protection to the industries of Canada, which he (Mr. Charlton) thought they should receive, used these words :
I had a great deal of pleasure a short time ago in listening to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), and I can endorse most fully his encomiums as to the good character of the administration of the Mackenzie government, and as to his speculations as to what would probably have been the outcome of that policy had they continued in power.
These remarks seem to be quite iuconsisteut with these other quotations from the speech of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) which

I have read to the House. How can he eulogize and endorse the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Kichard Cartwright) for the good acts of the Mackenzie government, when that gentleman held the portfolio of finance in that government; when he agreed with the hon. member (Mr. Charlton) that protection was necessary for the welfare of this country, but who, feeling that the interests of his party might be sacrificed if they gave that reasonable measure of protection which he believed in, denied his principles, stood beside his leader and refused to give the people what they desired and what was necessary for their welfare ?
Hear, hear.

Surely if Mr. Mackenzie is to be condemned, equally deserving of condemnation, is the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the laches of the government in that great crisis in the history of our country ? If I am rightly informed, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Ross) who sits on the left of the hon. member for Norfolk was a member of the Mackenzie government at that time, and he too is responsible for the action of that minister.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) No.

Then I have been misinformed.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) My last session was in 1874.

Then the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Ross) got out before the threat was made against the Mackenzie government by the members from the maritime provinces ? However, there are some living representatives of the Mackenzie cabinet in the cabinet of the present day. There is the right hon. the Prime Minister.
No.

I shall withdraw the accusation. I am glad that the right hon. Prime Minister is not responsible for the acts of the government of 1876; he has enough responsibility to assume for the acts of the present government. However, if the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross) and if the right hon. the Prime Minister were not members of the Mackenzie cabinet of that date, we have at all events the noblest Roman of them all; we have the Minister of Trade and Commerce who was certainly a member of the Mackenzie administration in 1876.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext:
Yes, and the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) must be held responsible for the acts of that government. But, instead of condemning that hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), we find the member for North Nor-Mr. CLARKE.
folk endorsing him and praising him, and congratulating* him on the speech he made in this House which he characterized as being a most ingenious deliverance. Well, It was an ingenious deliverance, and considering it from the standpoint of ingenuity alone, I join the member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) in congratulating the Minister of Trade and Commerce on that speech. But, Sir, between 1878 and 1896, let ns remember that these two hon. gentlemen (Sir Richard Cartwright and Mr. Charlton) went throughout this country declaring that the policy of the Liberal party was a policy of free trade; that the policy of the Liberal party was opposed to protection; and in face of that we have the admission to-day from the hon. member (Mr. Charlton) that they both favoured a substantial addition to the tariff of 1878, and that the reason they were not able to accomplish a change in the fiscal policy of the Mackenzie government, was because of the threat made by the Liberal representatives from the maritime provinces that if it were done they would withdraw their support.
I do not think, Sir, that the statement made by the hon. member (Mr. Charlton), is calculated to reflect credit on the character of the gentlemen who were concerned in the transaction, nor do I think it will add lustre to the achievements of the Liberal party of Canada. In what position is the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) 7 Let us consider for a moment his position. The hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) declares that he is a protectionist to the hilt, while his desk mate from Russell, a gentleman who has represented that constituency for many years in this House, declares himself to be a free trader to the hilt. From 1878 to 1896, the hon. member for North Norfolk sat in his place in this House, and he consistently voted against the principle of protection during all that time. He never neglected an opportunity of condemning that policy, and of condemning those who framed it and put it into operation. His colleague from Russell who was a free trader then and says he is a free trader now, was consistent up to 1896 in voting against the protective policy, but he now plays a role almost as inconsistent as that of his hon. friend (Mr. Charlton), for since 1896-ignoring the pledges of the Liberal party, ignoring their promise of retrenchment, ignoring their declaration that they would destroy the policy of protection-he has since that time been one of the most faithful and steadfast supporters of the Liberal party who certainly have not adopted anything remotely approaching a free trade policy. Let us see what changes the Liberals have made in the Conservative protective tariff since they came into power. The Finance Minister told us in his budget speech that while in 1896 the duty collected on all importa-

tions into Canada was equal to 18-28 per cent ; the duty collected in 1901 amounted 16-06 per cent. This statement shows us that a reduction of 2-22 per cent has been made by the Liberals on the tariff which was in existence in 1890, and under which tariff the Liberals out of office, said, the consumers and producers of this country were being robbed and crushed. A reduction was made in the Conservative tariff, therefore, only to the extent of 2-22 per cent, and the hon. member for Russell who still claims to be a free trader to the hilt, has no hesitation in supporting this government, and declaring by his vote that they have redeemed then- pledges, when on their own statement they have only made this miserable reduction of 2-22 per cent on the duties imposed by the tariff of 1896. And, Sir, this miserable pittance of 2-22 per cent, includes the so-called British preference; includes the so-called preference which was given to the motherland as a proof of fidelity and attachment to British institutions. At least, so the ministers of the day say. Well, Sir, if that so-called preference had not been given, the reduction which the Liberal government has made in the tariff would be much smaller even than 2-22 per cent.
The hon. member for North Norfolk, while professing for 18 years to be a free trader, has now practically admitted that he was a protectionist, and we are bound to accept his statement. But, surely, if he is sincere, he must take one more step ; he must dissociate himself from hon. gentlemen opposite, because he has given to us and the country the strongest possible evidence of their insincerity on this question of tariff reform. If the hon. gentleman believes in the principles he has enunciated, he certainly ought not longer to continue to support gentlemen who have no fixed principles respecting the tariff. We ought not to be surprised at the divergence of opinion that exists among the unofficial members of the Liberal party who occupy seats in this House, when we find so much divergence of opinion among the leaders of the party. We have had exhibitions of this'divergence of opinion among them again and again. At the great banquet of the Manufacturer's Association of Canada, held in Montreal a few months ago, the Premier took to himself the credit of having a tariff that was almost perfect He said :
I do not know, you know better than I do because you have to deal with it more than I do-it may be that there are blemishes in it ; but whether there are blemishes in it or not, I suppose on the whole the manufacturers are pretty well satisfied.
Upon several voices saying ' No, no,' the right hon. gentleman added :
That only shows that there is room for improvement.
Naturally exception was taken to the statement that the tariff was almost perfect,
and when the right hon. gentleman heard the cries of ' No, no,' he at once turned round and said, ' That only shows that there is room for improvement in it.' There is certainly a great deal of room for improvement in the tariff ; and if the resolution presented by the hon. leader of the opposition met with the approval of the members of this House, a decided improvement would be made in the tariff, and substantial benefit done to the interests of the country thereby. The Minister of Finance was also present at that banquet in Montreal, and he said :
A friend whom I met here to-night, an honoured member of your association, said ; I want the tariff to be out of politics.' So do I ; nay, more, I venture to say, and I hope I can say it without going beyond the line which no man should pass beyond at this non-political union, but I hope I can say that the tariff is largely out of politics to-day, and that if you will take the trouble to read the discussions at Ottawa you will come to the conclusion that-there is not much difference of opinion between the two great political parties in Canada upon this great question.
Sir, the resolution which has been submitted by the leader of the opposition proves that there is a substantial difference between the two parties on this question of tariff reform. If that difference is not greater at the present time, it is due to the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite have largely abandoned the position they held up to 1896, and have adopted the view of this side of the House, that a substantial measure of protection is necessary to the existence of the industries of the country. But there was another minister present at that banquet, and he gave no uncertain sound as to where he stood on this question of tariff reform. He said :
The United States takes us by the threat every time in trade matters. I cannot see why our Canadian customs should not be as self-protecting as theirs. (Cheers.)
I care not about words nor theories. The first principle is to defend ourselves. Do not think I belong to a government which thinks alike.
If we ever thought so, our minds have been disabused of that idea long ago. He went on :
You have no idea what a cabinet meeting is. They fight like blazes sometimes. (Loud laughter.) I have been brought up in a protectionist school and I have not renounced my faith.
That is the attitude of a gentleman who occupies a very prominent position in the government of this country to-day ; and I think I may say that that minister has no stauncher supporter in this House than the hon. member who represents the county of Russell (Mr. Edwards). We have thus the right hon. gentleman who occupies the position of premier claiming to be a free trader, and having associated with him in his cabi-

net men who are avowed out-and-out protectionists. This method of conducting the affairs of the country may he in accord with constitutional practice, but I think it is unique in the history of Canada.
The hon. member for North Norfolk referred to the Anglo American Commission. The important position that hon. gentleman occupies in the ranks of the Liberal party-or probably it would be fairer to say the important position he occupied in the ranks of the Liberal party two or three years ago-was seen in the fact that of all the able men in the party who are not members of the cabinet he was selected as the gentleman best qualified to deal with matters of such vital importance as those affecting the relations of Canada with the United States. He was selected from amongst all the followers of the government to become associated with two or three members of the cabinet in dealing with these perplexing questions. That hon. gentleman knows in his heart of hearts that if he were as frank on this subject as he was yesterday in declaring his protectionist principles he would tell this House that when that commission went to Washington, they were utterly at sea as to the wants and requirements of this country, and that he himself had very largely to prepare the statistics on which the commission depended for information as to the trade and trade interests of this country. These gentlemen were as indefatigable as their predecessors in endeavouring to bring about a settlement of the questions at issue between Canada and the United States ; but what was the result of all their meetings ? Practically nothing, and yet the hon. gentleman said in his speech yesterday :
The condition of trade between these two countries at the present time warrants us in saying to the United States : Give us reciprocity in natural products. Not that we will promise you any mitigation of our tariff system. We will not agree to put a single article more on the free list. We will not agree to reduce our duties unless we choose to do so, we are entitled on the basis of the conditions as they are to-day to reciprocity in natural products.
Although that commission met again and again and failed to accomplish anything, and although the right hon. premier said it was not going to Washington any more, yet the hon. member for North Norfolk thinks that they ought to go once more. For what purpose ? To try to negotiate a reciprocity treaty in natural products alone. He says :
But I am anxious to see that Joint High Commission meet once more. I am anxious to ascertain, as a result of that meeting, whether these questions can be satisfactorily adjusted or not. When we have definitely ascertained one way or the other, we shall know what course we ought to pursue ; and if we cannot get fair play, we can at least place ourselves in a position where we shall not receive the

to make a like repeal of its duties upon merchandise, the products of the United States.
That statement is made by Mr. Osborne Howe. He declares that Mr. Dingley agreed to make a recommendation to congress to give us free access to the American markets provided we gave the Americans free access to our markets. Mr. Howe said further :
The present needs of revenue from the customs, and the discrimination which a practical carrying out of this plan would have made against imports coming from England, were considered by the Canadian commissioners to be sufficient justification for their refusal to favourably entertain this proposition. In effect it would have involved the adoption by Canada of the tariff system of the United States with a sensible loss of legislative independence. The sessions of the Joint High Commission apparently came to an end in consequence of an insuperable disagreement over the question of the Alaska boundary line ; but it is inherently probable that a method would have been found of compromising this difference if satisfactory headway had been made towards coming together for the formation of a reciprocal trade treaty. In the absence of this centripetal influence, it seemed, when a contention arose over the boundary question, that there was nothing to be gained by prolonged and inconclusive discussions, hence the sessions came to an end.
That is the statement made in this journal, the ' Expansionist,' by Mr. Osborne ITowe, as to the real reason why the commission, appointed at the instance of hon. gentlemen opposite, came to naught. And in 1899, under date March 24th, I find in the London ' Times ' this paragraph :
That Canada alone has much to gain from a satisfactory settlement of the trade and boundary questions in dispute is an entirely fallacious presentment of the case. The interests of the United States are quite as deeply involved as those of her continental neighbours, and many of the well informed advisors of .the Canadian government perceiving this to be the case are exerting pressure rather to bring about a rupture of the negotiations than to contribute a settlement.
The hon. member for North Norfolk knows whether these statements are justified or not, but I would not be at all surprised, when the secret history of these negotiations comes to be known, to learn that there were other matters besides the Alaskan boundary question, upon which a very substantial disagreement took place between the commissioners of both countries.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

House in Committee on Bill (No. 21) respecting the Port Dover, Brantford, Berlin Mr. CLARKE.
and Goderich Railway Company and to change its name to ' The Grand Valley Traction Company.'-Mr. Heyd.
On section 1.
Will the chairman of the committee (Mr. Hyman) kindly explain the changes made in this Bill.

The original Bill included a section, numbered four, to which some objection was taken by the committee on the ground that it allowed different bonding privileges in regard to different sections of the road. The committee felt that that was not in accordance with the usual custom ; and, after consideration it was withdrawn by the promoters. Then, under the last clause of the Bill, the company were asking for an extension of seven years, and the committee decided to give them an extension of two years to commence and five years to complete.
The bonding privileges, I understand, extend to the whole road ?

Yes. just as they were originally.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill (No. 24) respecting the Windsor and Detroit Union Bridge Company.-Mr. Cowan.
On section 1.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: Will the chairman of the committee please explain the changes in this Bill ?

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: The original Bill proposed an extension of five and seven years. The committee, in accordance with the precedent that they have established in other bills of a like character, gave the committee five years to complete.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: And how many to commence ?

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: I may say that there were two other Bills practically of the same character considered by the committee, and as they were bridge Bills it was thought by the committee that the companies would be entitled to five years from the passing of the act. In the case of this particular company, it is really only four years, bcause they have come here almost a year before the expiration of their powers under their original charter.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: There is no time fixed for commencement.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: No, but-

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: How then, is the time for commencement fixed ?

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: May I be allowed to explain ? The company have to commence within two years from the time they receive powers-this being an international work-from the congress of the United States. And, to limit them, so that the charter may not be held if the conditions change, or the mind of this House should change regarding the granting of these powers, they have to complete the work within five years of that time. They have to commence within two years, which is our rule. They really have no existence and canaot do anything until they have acquired joint legislation from the United States.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. James Sutherland).

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: There is nothing about when they are to commence.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: What is provided for in the charter is that they must commence within two years, and they cannot commence until they acquire legislation from the United States Congress. After they acquire that power, at any rate, they must complete the work within five years or return to this parliament for a renewal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: The minister says that our rule is that they commence within two years, but our rule has no force after this statute passes. We are amending the whole statute. Some of the other Acts which we passed provide that within two years after they got their charter from the American authorities they must commence work, and they must finish it within five years. This specifies it must be finished within five years, but says nothing with regard to when it shall commence after they get their authority from the United States.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: I think that is provided for in the original charter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: We are amending that clause of the charter which relates to the beginning and finishing of the road, and after that is passed, it is the only law which will govern, I assume.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: ' Perhaps the bridge is commenced.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: No, the bridge is not commenced. The committee most carefully considered this whole matter, looking upon the undertaking as somewhat different from a railway company; and it being an international measure and dependent upon legislation from the United States, it was felt that five years ought to be put in instead of two. It might be impossible to get legislation within one year, and probably they are getting no more than they are entitled to in that sense.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: We have not taken that view with regard to these Bills heretofore. We have always made their commencement contingent upon legislation in the United States, because that Act might be passed early or late, but it commenced to count from the time of passing.	.

subtopic: WINDSOR AND DETROIT UNION BRIDGE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am inclined to think, and I thought when I spoke before, that the charter was not amended, and had the ori- . ginal clause providing that they must commence two years after they receive their authority from the United States Congress. But the clause as drawn by the promoters of the Bill, I think, would meet the views of the hon. gentleman for this reason, that the work has to be built within five years from the granting of this charter, otherwise it becomes null and void. So they have only five years to procure legislation and finish the work. That is stricter than other Bills.

But such substitution shall not :n any way impair, alter or affect the liabilities of the Buffalo Railway Company, uor in any wise affect any suit or proceeding now pending, or judgment existing either by, or in favour of, or against the company, which notwithstanding such substitution may be prosecuted, continued, completed and enforced as if this Act had not been passed.
