House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) :
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply io be granted to His Majesty and the proposed motion of Mr. Borden (Halifax) in amendment thereto.
['BELL (Pictou) moved the adjournment of the debate.']

Mr. Speaker, when you left the Chair at six o'clock, I had been drawing the attention of the House to the position occupied by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and to the statement which he made respecting his relations to the adoption of a moderate policy of protection. He declared that he bad favoured in 1876 a moderate policy of protection, a policy such as had been introduced by the Conservative party and carried in 1878 or 1879, while at the same time he steadily offered opposition to that policy from its adoption down to 1896. I was also drawing attention to the fact that, from the statement made by the hon. member for North Norfolk, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) was practically in the same position, and I quoted an extract from a speech delivered by the right bon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) on the occasion of a banquet tendered to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1900, to the effect that the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce had also favoured a moderate measure of protection, but, that he had been overruled, or coerced, by his colleagues in the House who then occupied seats and represented constituencies in the maritime provinces ; that from the adoption of that policy of protection down to 1896 he had been denouncing it, notwithstanding the allegation that prior to 1878 he had favoured it. I also referred to the statement made, and repeated again and again, that the Liberal party had declared that Canada could enjoy no general or real measure of prosperity unless and until we had obtained access to the markets of the great republic to the south of us for our surplus agricultural products; that the Liberal party had charged that the Conservative delegates, who went to Washington again and

again to try to secure a treaty that would enlarge trade between the two countries, did not go with the desire or the intention of being successful, because they had confined their efforts to offers of restricted reciprocity when the Liberal party, had declared that it was impossible to make any agreement with the statesmen of the United States except on the basis of unrestricted reciprocity. I quoted also from a statement of the ' Expansionist ' newspaper to the effect that Mr. Dingley had favoured the passage of a measure through the congress of the United States that would provide for the free admission of Canadian products to the markets of that country on condition of our granting them a like privilege by the admission of American products free into the markets of Canada, but that the proposition had been declined. I may say here, Mr. Speaker, that, speaking for myself, and I believe, speaking for every lion, gentleman on this side of the House, if the Canadian commissioners who visited Washington in 1898, or 1899, were offered unrestricted reciprocity and refused fo accept it, upon the conditions that I have named, they acted well and wisely in the interests of the country, because, I think it was better that in that case, as in many other cases that might be cited, that party should abandon its position rather than that the interests of the country should be sacrificed. I attribute their change of policy to the fact that having come into office, they realized the responsibility attaching to their position, they realized to a greater extent than previously that Canada has as much to lose as to gain by the adoption of the policy of unrestricted reciprocity, that Canada has as much to give as to obtain from that policy ; and that having committed themselves to this policy of a so-called British preference they could not meet the views or wishes of their American colleagues on that Joint High Commission.
There are no two opinions to-day as to the fact that the country is prosperous. We rejoice in that fact and we can congratulate the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) in being able to make the statement he made the other day as to the prosperity of the country. We hope that prosperity will continue for many years to come, but, we challenge the accuracy of the statements which have been made from time to time by hon. gentlemen opposite as to their part in bringing about that prosperity. We have invited them to make a statement as to what they have done to promote the prosperity of the country. Have they lowered the taxation of the people of this country ? On the contrary, taxation has been very much larger than it was before they assumed office. They have not provided any new markets for the surplus products of the farmers of this country. Our farmers still find their market in the old land. They are not selling as much of their products in the United
States ; they certainly are not selling more in the United States than they did prior to 1896, while larger quantities of American food products are brought into Canada now than then. I invite hon. gentlemen on the other side, to point us to a single item of their policy by which they have provided any markets in addition to those in existence in 1896. I defy them to point to any such policy. Our Canadian farmers have been steadily cultivating the British market-a market which the Liberals out of power declared to be a second hand and second rate market. And, Sir, it was because the farmers of Canada turned a deaf ear to the representations made to them by the Liberals prior to 1896, and accepted the advice given by the leaders of the Conservative party, that they should cultivate the British market because it was the best and safest and likely to be the most abiding ; it is due to that fact that we have such a development of trade with the English market to-day. The substantial increase which has taken place in the sale of Canadian agricultural products on the British market, has amply justified the predictions made by the Conservative party and has confounded the pessimistic prophecies made by the Liberals before they attained power.
And, Sir, to what is the present prosperity of Canada to be attributed ? What have the Liberal government done to contribute to that prosperity ? What policy have they put into force which would tend to make us prosper ? Sir, the prosperity which has obtained on the American continent during these past five or six years, is due to other causes, and is not due to any policy propounded by the Canadian government. Let me quote the opinion of an American author on this point. He says :
Prosperity must always begin with the producer. Something must be obtained _ from the soil which can be sold for money.
Canada has prospered since 1896 because of a succession of abundant harvests, because of the cultivation of a larger area of her fertile lands in the North-west, and because of other things which I shall take occasion to enumerate. The figures prepared by the Bureau of Statistics at Toronto reveal a wonderful condition. If you take the value of Ontario field crops, and of animals and j their products, in 1896, and compare it with the value of the same products from 1897 to 1901, the gratifying fact is shown that while these products in 1896 were valued at $125,813,000, the average yearly value from 1897 to 1901 has been not less than $156,570,000, or, in other words, the agricultural products of Ontario have been worth $30,000,000 a year more from 1897 to the present date, than they were in 1896. That is a very substantial reason why this country has been blessed with great prosperity during the later period. If we take into consideration the further fact, that larger areas

of land have been placed under cultivation in Manitoba and the North-west territories, we can realize why the volume of business has been steadily increasing from that part of our Dominion. There have been valuable discoveries and exploitations of mineral lands since 1896 ; the wonderful riches of the Klondike have been developed, and all these causes combined have brought about our prosperity. Is it not strange that hon. gentlemen opposite do not hesitate to take to themselves practically all the credit for this improved condition of things ? I fancy that if they compared the improvement which has taken place in the United States with the improvement which has taken place in Canada, these gentlemen would not be so ready to congratulate themselves as they are. What has been the cause of the prosperity in the United States during the same period ? You will recollect that as late as 1894 the condition of things in that great country was such as to cause general alarm-trade was prostrated ; banks were failing every day, large industrial institutions were being closed. This unsatisfactory condition was due to a general depression, to the lack of a ready and profitable sale for the surplus food products of the country, and because of the failure of crops in certain sections. Let me quote to you the opinion of Mr. R. S. Baker, who has written very fully on the development of the trade of the United States, and on the causes which have led to the prosperity there since 1896. He says :
Ifc is curious and wonderful to see iiow exactly the industries of the world tread in lock-step, and how the man of the soil, the farmer, towers huge and powerful at the head of the line. When his tread is slow and heavy, the iron master, the transporter, the miner, the manufacturer, must also tread slowly-and depression and hard times are abroad in the land. But when the man of the soil increases his speed, those behind him move more rapi'dly ; for he represents the worlds primary ne;d-food.
In the fall of 1897 there was an enormous crop of wheat in the United States, the largest by all odds in many years. At the same time the wheat crops in Russia and India were short, to the verge of famine in the last named country, and the great consumsrs of Europe, England especially, were compelled to turn to America for food to a much greater extent than usual.
Then in the fall of 1898 came another amazing wheat crop, more than 075,000,000 bushels, the largest wheat crop in the history of America.
There were also large and richly profitable ci rn and oat crops, and the south raised the greatest crop of cotton in its history, rising from 8,700,000 bales In 1837 to upwards of 11,000,000 bales in 1898.
The author of this work on the prosperity of the United States goes on to show what followed:
In less than three years time, between 1897 and 1900, so great were the trade balances in our favour that over a billion dollars of American indebtedness was wiped from the ledgers of Europe. Wages for laDour increased rapidly in every part of the country, and never was

there such a sudden and yet substantial expansion in the various manufacturing industries.
In the single state of Kansas, the farm ,mortgages which in 1890 amounted to the vast sum of $240,000,030, much of it bearing the exorbitant interest of 12 per cent, had been reduced in 1899 to less than $41,000,000.
On June 30, 1899, there were over 5,200,000 depositors in savings banks in the United States compared with 4,800,000 in 1894 and 3,500,000 in 1889, a gain of 1,400,000 in ten years. And each of these depositors had more money to his account than ever before, the average amount on deiosit rising from $339 for each person in 1894 to $419 in 1899.
The deposits in all the banks, national and state, as well as savings, repr.e-j snting upwards of 13,000,000 individual depositors, actually doubled in ten years, amounting in 1899 to the enormous sum of $7,514,000,000.
In 1893 no fewer than 74 railroad companies, representing the vast sum of $1,781,000,300 in stocks and. bonds, went to the wall, and there were large numbers of failures in 1894, 1895 and 1896. In 1899, there were failures of only 10 roads with a little more than $50,000,000 in stocks and bonds, the best record by all odds since 1882.
A glance at the number of commercial failures will show how they decreased, from over 15.000 in 1893, with an enormous total of liabilities of nearly $347,000,000, to only 9,337 failures in 1899 with liabilities of less than $91,000.000.
If time permitted I might quote further reasons for that great prosperity in the United States, which has been brought about because of the redundant harvests which have blessed that country, because of the shortage of the crops in other parts of the world. The same reasons for our prosperity have obtained in this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not give credit for the prosperity to these causes, but they exultantly exclaim that Canada has made more progress during the last five years tiiari during the previous twenty years, if they made a comparison of the trade of Canada with I he trade of the United States durine (lie same period we might not have so much reason to complain of their attitude in this respect.
But Canada has been prosperous and would have been prosperous without the assistance of hon. gentlemen opposite. The splendid harvests we have had would have caused the measure of prosperity we have enjoyed. The test of the soundness of the fiscal policy of this country is to be found rather in the condition which obtained in Canada from 1891 to 1896, when a period of universal depression prevailed throughout this continent. If hon. gentlemen will examine the record of the trade of Canada from 1891 to 1896, and compare it with the record of the trade of the United States for the same period, they will find that, slow as was the growth of this country, it was more satisfactory and substantial in proportion to our population than was the growth of the great republic to the south of us. In 1891 the total imports and exports of Canada amounted to $218,385,000, and for the

next five years-that period of universal depression from 1892 to 1896-the average annual trade of Canada amounted to $238,690,000, an increase of $20,000,000 per annum during each year of that period of depression.
Now, let us turn to the trade statistics of the United States for the same period. In 1891 the imports and exports of the Republic amounted to $1,729,397,000, and for the next five years-1892, 1893, 1891, 1895 and 1896-there was no increase in the trade of the country. On the contrary, there was a decline of $65,000,000 per annum, the average annual imports and exports for the period being $1,664,144,000.
But hon. gentlemen say that Canada has made more progress in the last five years than she made in the preceding twenty years. Let us examine the recorcT of Canada's trade for the fifteen years from 1881 to 1896. In 1881 the imports and exports of Canada amounted to $189,902,427, and for the succeeding fifteen years that trade averaged $211,537,804 per annum ; in other words, it showed during that period an annual increase of nearly $22,000,000 over the total trade of the year 1881.
Now, we have heard a good deal about the prosperity of the United States. Let us make a comparison between the prosperity which obtained in Canada from 1881 to 1896 and the prosperity which obtained in the United States during the same period. In 1881 the total value of the United States imports and exports of merchandise was $1,545,041,974, while for the succeeding fifteen years up to 1896, the average trade of the Republic was $1,538,553,125. In other words, while the trade of Canada during that period of fifteen years showed an average annual increase of $22,000,00, the trade of the United States showed an average annual decline of no less than $6,500,000. If the policy which prevailed in Canada from 1891 to *1896, when depression was universal, enabled this country not only to hold its own, but to make reasonable progress, that fact affords the strongest possible evidence we can have as to the wisdom and the patriotism of those who framed the fiscal policy which then existed in this country.
But we have heard a great deal of the progress which has obtained in Canada since 1896. When hon. gentlemen opposite make a statement of that kind, they take good care not to tell us of the progress made in other countries during the same period. They used to be very fond of quoting statistics to show the progress of the United States. Let us look at the statistics of the trade of that country since 1896. We have seen that for the fifteen years prior to that year the average annual imports and exports of merchandise in the United States amounted to $1,538,553,125. The annual average during the five years since then has been no less a sum than $2,028,557,833, or an average annual increase of no less than
$490,004,708. This is the strongest possible proof we can give of the enormous expansion which has taken place in the trade of that country during that period. The im-irorts and exports of merchandise in the United States were $190,000,000 less in 1895 than they were in 1891, while they were $771,429,026 greater in 1901 than they were in 1895, an expansion equal to double the total value of the imports and exports of Canada in the past year.
But, Sir, this marvellous expansion was not confined to Canada or the United States. Let me quote a few figures to show how the trade of the United Kingdom expanded during the same period. I shall have to take the statistics from 1891 to 1900, because these are the latest I could get in the library. In 1891 the exports and imports of the United Kingdom amounted to $3,618,537,000 ; in 1893 they dropped down to $3,313,676,000, and in 1894 to $3,315,154,000 ; in 1896 they climbed up to $3,587,253,000; while in 1900 they amounted to the enormous sum of $4,207,974,000. The trade of the United Kingdom for 1900 exceeded that for 1894 by the enormous sum of $950,000,000, while the trade for 1900 exceeded the trade for 1896 by the sum of $680,000,000.
It is a singular fact that during the year 1891 Lord Salisbury was in office ; it was the last full year in which he was premier prior to the advent of Mr. Gladstone. He was succeeded by Mr. Gladstone in 1892. The first full year of Mr. Gladstone was 1893. He was followed by Lord Rosebery in 1894, and Lord Rosebery was in turn succeeded by Lord Salisbury in 1895. In 1891, as I have pointed out, the total imports and exports of the United Kingdom amounted to $3,618,537,000.
During the first year of Mr. Gladstone's administration they decreased more than $300,000,000. The same story was told during the administration of Lord Rosebery. But after Lord Salisbury attained office, succeeding both Liberal premiers, the trade of the United Kingdom went up again by leaps and bounds. Yet we have never heard, either in Canada or Hie old land, that anybody attached any blame to Mr. Gladstone because of the shrinkage of trade after he assumed office or gave any particular credit to Lord Salisbury because of the enormous expansion of trade which took place since he assumed the premiership in the latter' end of 1895. But hon. gentlemen opposite would like to make us believe that, by some political sleight of hand, they have been able to increase the trade of this country in the gratifying proportions in which it has increased from 1896 up to the present.
Let me point out that the wonderful expansion of trade which has taken place in the United States during the past five years has been rendered possible by the attention the Americans have given to the all important question of transportation. Mr. Baker, whose work on the prosperity of the United States I have already quoted, declares that a bushel of wheat, or an equivalent quantity of flour, can be shipped from Minneapolis to almost any point in western Europe for about 20 cents. This includes no fewer than three transhipments-at Duluth, Buffalo and New York ; and that it costs almost as much to ship the same wheat from Liverpool to Manchester, in England.
The Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) claims to be seized with the importance of this question of transportation. Might I ask him what scheme he has devised and perfected for the improvement of our transportation facilities ? It is true that we have had the Intercolonial Railway brought into Montreal. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said that when the Liberal party came into office in 1896, they found the western terminus of the Intercolonial Railway in a ploughed field. Well, what special advantage has come to the taxpayers of Canada by reason of its having been extended to Montreal? Are the taxpayers, are the producers of the country, getting any benefit from the extension of the Intercolonial Railway into that city ? If we examine the returns of the past year, I do not think we will find there any matter for congratulation. It seems to me it would have been better had these hon. gentlemen left the western terminus of the Intercolonial Railway in a ploughed field rather than incur the enormous expense and reap the meagre returns from that expenditure, which are shown in the Public Accounts.
We have heard a great deal about making Montreal the national port. For two or three years past we have been listening to schemes for the construction of additional wharfage and the erection of additional elevators and the equipment of that port generally. Well, I would like to know what has become of the Conners syndicate elevator scheme ? We ha(1 tllat on t]ie boards two or three years ago, but there seems to be nothing left of it now. We also had another proposition some time ago for the construction of elevators, which also seems to have fallen through; and the present condition of things in our so-called national port cannot be at all satisfactory, if we are to pay any attention to the statements made by those well qualified to judge. I take the liberty of reading to the House an extract from the address of the retiring President of the Board of Trade oi Montreal, Mr. Henry Miles, delivered a few weeks ago. Wliat does lie say with regard to the equipment of the Montreal harbour :
In regard to the equipment of our harbour the position is unsatisfactory. The attitude pre-yafling in the direction of these affairs is such that I fear the alienation of the sympathies of parliament from our national port. Nothing has actually been accomplished towards this Mr. CLARKE.
equipment, and the idea of a * free port ' is submerged for the time being. Differences of opinion and contention, I would like to see put to one side ; let us have the work proceed.
There is a great common interest involved, the welfare of the commerce of the country and of the welfare of our city. We have a right to demand the setting aside of everything that appears to delay the accomplishment of success in this great national undertaking.
The position of affairs in the port of Montreal must be a serious one or the retiring President of the Board of Trade would never have given utterance to the words I have just read. It is time something definite was done, some scheme of transportation laid out and completed. We have silent hundreds of thousands of dollars pottering here and there throughout the country, but no plan has yet been adopted which has given the producers of the west the slightest relief or assistance.
Does the management of our government railways during the past few years give any cause for rejoicing to those who advocate the nationalization of our railways, telegraphs and telephone lines ? From 1892 to 1896, we spent on capital account on the Intercolonial Railway $1,643,074.65, and on the Prince Edward Island Railway $8,300.49, making a total expenditure from 1892 to 1896 on capital account of $1,651,375.14, and during those five years we lost in the operation of those two roads $943,552. Since hon. gentlemen opposite came into office what do the figures show ? They show that the expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway from 1897 to 1901 on capital account amounted to the enormous sum of $8,414,441.21, and on the Prince Edward Island Railway $373,201.83. Or, in the past five years, we have spent on capital account on both these lines, $8,787,703.04, and during those years we lost no less than $901,424 in the operation of those roads. In other words, in round figures, in the last ten years, we have spent over $10,000,000 on capital account on these two railways, and the receipts have fallen almost $2,000,000 short of the actual expenses in connection with their operation.
I would like to know how much longer this condition is going to last ? Are we to go on spending, on an average $1,000,000 a year on capital account, more than one-half of which should be charged to operating expenses, and lose besides from $300,000 to $600,000 per year in the operation of these roads ? It might be some consolation to us if we knew that our brothers down by the sea were getting some advantage in the shape of cheap freight and passenger rates, but I am told that the schedules of the Intercolonial Railway show that while the people of the maritime provinces have to stand, in common with the other provinces, an annual loss in the operation of the government roads, they are charged at least as much for freight and passenger service as are those served by

roads not under tlie control or management of the government.
I wish now to refer briefly to the so-called British preference which is mentioned in the amendment presented by the hon. the leader of the opposition. I may say that the idea of giving a preference to the workingmen and the manufacturers of the old land was a rather popular idea. It seemed to be appreciated and accepted as a good policy by the great majority of Canadians, when that policy was inaugurated. But it was hoped that when the Liberal party came into office-accepting- the statement of the right hon. gentleman who is now premier as being made in good faith-an effort would be made to secure for the products of Canada some preference in the markets of the old land. But, unfortunately, in that matter, as in many others, we were doomed to be disappointed. We know, that, in 1896, the premier declared in London that it would be a good thing to obtain a mutual preference, and that when the Liberal party should get into power they would send commissioners to try to obtain that mutual preference. Well, twelve months after, when the Prime Minister was on his way to attend the Jubilee in London, in 1897, he practically declined to accept any preference. He said :
I claim for the present government of Canada that they have passed a resolution by which the products of Great Britain are admitted on the rate of their tariff, at 12J per cent, and next year at 25 per cent reduction. This we have done, not asking any compensation.
There is a class of our fellow citizens who ask that all such concessions should be made for ' quid pro quo.'
The Canadian government has ignored all such sentiments.
We have done it because we owe a debt of gratitude to Great Britain. We have done it because it is no intention of ours to disturb in any way the system of free trade which has done so much for England.
What we give you by our tariff we give you in gratitude for the splendid freedom under which we have prospered. It is a free gift. We ask no compensation. Protection has been the curse of Canada. We would not see you come under its baneful influence-for what weakens you must weaken us.
That is the statement made by the right hon. gentleman at Liverpool, in June, 1897. On the 6th of October following, speaking in the city of Toronto, he declared
If I had thought I could have obtained for the products of Canada preferential treatment in the markets of Great Britain, not only would I have been wanting in patriotism, but I would have been wanting in reason. I would have been simply an idiot if I had not obtained such preference for the products of Canada.
Sir, it is a difficult thing to reconcile these two statements. But we were disappointed, to say the least of it, when the distinguished Canadian who represented Canada on the occasion of the Jubilee did not make more 52
strenuous efforts to obtain for the farmers and other producers In Canada some advantage in return for the advantages which, he claimed, the Canadian government had given to the manufacturers and workmen of the mother country. He entertained the view that he was giving something to Great Britain. But the Minister of Finance (Hon. W. S. Fielding) who, probably, knew better the effect of what was being done, said that they were giving nothing. He said
We do not by our resolutions offer anything to Great Britain alone. We recognize the fact that Great Britain by her liberal policy is in a position to avail herself of this offer immediately, but we make our offer not to Great Britain only, but to every nation which is prepared to accept it. We make it to every country which is willing to establish fair and reasonable trade relations with Canada.
And the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce said :-
I say with respect to the offer we now make, that it is not a preferential offer at all in the true legal sense of the word. That offer is open to all the world. The Americans may avail themselves of it and so may the Germans and the Belgians.
And from all the statistics I have seen, the Germans and the Belgians are availing themselves of It.
The whole world are welcome to avail themselves of it on the same terms and the same conditions on which England may take advantage of it. Where is the pref jrence there ?
Where is the preference there ? In 1901, according to the statement made by an hon. gentleman since this debate began, the average rate of duty on all imports coming in from the United States was 12-05. while the percentage on all goods from Great Britain was 18-23, notwithstanding this wonderful preference. The British imports paid half as much more duty as the imports from the United States. And, if you take the dutiable imports entered for consumption in 1901, you find that, while the average rate from the United States was 24 83, the average rate on goods from Great Britain was 24-74. So nicely had the tariff been arranged before this so-called British preference came into force, that it was found and is found to-day that the average rate on dutiable goods from Great Britain is practically the same as that on dutiable goods from the United States, notwithstanding the so-called preference.
But we have testimony as to the effect of this preference, from a gentleman whose qualification to express an opinion will not be challenged in this House. We have the statement of the gentleman who' was, and, I believe still is, the secretary of that great free trade organization, the Cobden Club, from which the right hon. premier deigned to accept a medal because of his services to the empire in giving this so-called British preference.



Writing to the ' London Times ' on September 30th, 1898, this gentleman said
The two great competitors for the Canadian market are the United Kingdom and the United States. In spite of the so-called British preferential tariff, the proportion of the total trade secured by the United States continues to increase and the proportion secured by the United Kingdom continues to decline. The explanation of this fact is that the bulk of the goods exported from the United States to Canada are admitted free, whereas the bulk of the goods exported from the United Kingdom are heavily taxed. The Canadian financial policy is to encourage the trade of the United States and not that of the United King iom.
That is the deliberate statement of the secretary of the Cobden Club. And we are asked to continue to endorse and sustain that which, according to this statement, contributes to increase the volume of trade with the United States and to decrease proportionately that from the mother country. In 1901, the free goods from the United States were valued at $56,884,730, while for the same year the free goods from Great Britain amounted to $11,316,510. The more you tinker with tariffs the more you will have to tinker with them. I believe the tariff policy of a government should be on a solid foundation, because if you change the tariff from time to time it creates unrest in the country and leads to very injurious results to our general trade. The amendment of the leader of the opposition speaks of a ' declared policy,' and when the Conservative party in Canada makes the announcement that they are going to do such and such a thing, and when they declare that they will carry out a certain policy when they get into power, the people of Canada may rest assured that the Conservatives will carry out their pledges. The Conservatives differ from the Liberals in that respect it will bo noticed. I have often been asked why it is that wages are higher now than they were when Sir John Macdonald was in power. That 1 can answer easily. Sir John Macdonald built the Canadian Pacific Railway, and he opened the rich lands of Manitoba and the North-west to which our young men and \	young women in the older provinces are going, thus creating in the older provinces a scarcity of labour. That is one reason why wages are high now. Another reason is that the war in South Africa has taken away a number of our young men, and that money is being circulated in this country for the purposes of war supplies, giving increased employment, and so this war, unfortunate in many respects, has been to that extent a benefit to us. Not one of these gentlemen opposite has been honest enough to acknowledge the part that the war in South Africa has played in contributing to our present prosperity. Now, Sir, I cannot see for the life of me why politicians should not be as honest as clergymen. I believe that every man should be honest. Was not Sir John Macdonald an example of honesty in public life ? For years and years he devoted his life to the conduct of the affairs of this country, and he died in harness, a poor man without a dollar in the bank. There was a man to be looked up to by the people of Canada. Where will you find a clergyman of any denomination more honest than he V But what do you see going on to-day. Why, we see gentlemen on the other side of the House dodging and shifting from one position to the other. We see some members of the government holding different views from the other ministers. We see one Liberal getting up in the House to announce a policy utterly at variance with the policy announced by his leader. That is not honest, and I venture to think that the leader of the government does not believe that it is honest. When he sees one of his supporters rising in the House and shaking his hand at him as much as to say : I will not follow you, but when the vote comes voting blindly for whatever the Liberal party announces, what opinion can the right hon. gentleman have of such a man. I hope, Sir, that the time will come when the Conservative party will be in power with a declared policy, such as is announced in the resolution of the hon. leader of the opposition, for which I shall have much pleasure in "voting. Mr. FRANK OLIVER (Alberta). Mr. Speaker, this debate has taken a strange turn and a wide range. It has become the occasion of the profession of political faith as regards trade and tariff matters. I The House has had some surprises in that connection. We have found that certain geutlemen, who we supposed held fixed views in regard to tariff questions for many years, not only do not holu these .views now, but that they never held them. The House was surprised to hear that statement from one gentleman of prominence, and for my part I must refuse to that hon. gentleman the merit of inconsistency which he claimed for himself. He was not inconsistent, on his own showing. He was not inconsistent in his belief; he

dustries which really are the foundation of the greatness of our country.
1 was struck very much by the powerful arguments brought to bear on this as well as on the other side of the House, in favour of an increased tariff on imported manufactures. 1 was struck by the argument which went to prove the tremendous preponderance of wealth and manufacturing enterprise in the United States. It was held out to us that we must increase our protection or our country would be made a slaughter market by the manufacturers of the United States. That was the argument, but really, reading between the lines, following that argument out in detail, it struck me that the trouble was not at all with the manufacturers of the United States but with the manufacturers of Britain, under the British preference which prevails to-day. And that while our hon. friends were proclaiming themselves in favour of Britain, and possibly to some extent of British preference, they were really trying to get public sentiment worked up in favour of a high tariff, so that the British preference would be put an end to. They were using arguments against the United States for the purpose of raising an additional tariff in all against England. Did any of these gentlemen who held out to us so strongly the danger of our makets being slaughtered by the products of the United States advocate the desirability of a retaliatory tariff against the United States which would not apply to the rest of the world ? They did not. The idea was that we should retaliate against the United States by protecting ourselves against Britain.
Now, a word as to the extent to which the manufacturers of the United States are slaughtering their goods in Canada. Let us take, first, the case of agricultural implements. The sales in Canada of agricultural implements made in tiie United States are increasing greatly, they are increasing greatly in the North-west. In the town in which I live, there are four implement agencies, two representing Canadian manufacturers and two representing American manufacturers. All four are doing a good business. And to-day the American harvester, the McCormick or the Deering, is worth just ten dollars more than the Massey or the Frost and Wood implement in that town. Do you call that slaughtering the American product in the Canadian market I do not. To-day, I am credibly informed, our friends of the Imperial-otherwise the Standard-Oil Company are peddling oil throughout the towns of Ontario in doublebarrelled tank wagons. In one barrel is Canadian oil. and in the other is Amer-can oil. And the American oil costs the consumer just five cents 'a gallon more than the Canadian oil-jukt the amount of the duty. Mr. Speaker. Is American oil being slaughtered in the Canadian market to the detriment of Canadian oil ? We have

heard a good deal in previous sessions of the necessity of protecting the shirt and collar manufacturers in Montreal. There was some inequality in the tariff-I do not know what it was-that had to be adjusted in favour of these people, otherwise, they would be driven out of business because the Canadian market was being slaughtered by the foreign manufacturers. I happened in to a store on Sparks Street the other day to make a purchase. I was anxious to patronize Canadian industry, but the merchant who kept the store said he did not keep Canadian goods; that he kept only German and English goods. I found, on further inquiry, that I could buy a Canadian-made shirt for seventy-five cents; and my friend who did not keep Canadian goods, and who was doing business right along was selling English and Austrian-made goods for $1.25 to $1.50. Were these goods being slaughtered on the Canadian market V Now, let us have a word with our friends the manufacturers- just a word-with regard to this matter. These three lines of goods that I have mentioned-and I take it that they are only sample cases of the whole line of manufactures-are sold in Canada at higher prices than the Canadian products. Why V Simply because the Canadian product is inferior. There is no getting away from that conclusion. Why is the Canadian product inferior V Is it because the Canadian is not equal in skill to the Austrian, or the Britisher, or the American ? Is it because there is not sufficient capital in Canada to carry out these enterprises ? The Bank of Montreal lends money by the million in the city of Chicago and the city of New York, and is not the only Canadian bank that does so. Then, why are not the Canadian manufactures as good as the foreign ? There is no cause but that the Canadian manufacturer went into business, in many cases, with the intention of making his profit out of the tariff and not out of his business, and because he was able to come back year after year to this House and get the protection he saw fit to claim. He did not consider that he had to manufacture in competition with the outside, and he did not do it, nor is he doing it to-day. And, until the manufacturer of Canada rises to the occasion and uses the mechanical skill that is here, uses the capital that is here, uses the opportunity that is here to give the Canadian customer as good an article as tlwft customer can buy from the outside, lie is not entitled to protective consideration by this" House. I said a minute ago that I was a protectionist. I am a protectionist , and when Canada becomes a slaughter market for another country I shall be prepared to consider measures to prevent that from taking place. But that is not taking place to-day ; we are not even in danger of it taking place to-day. It is Britain that is selling us cheap goods

and not the United States. And when these men come to us and ask an increase of tariff in favour of their manufactures, they are using false arguments, as I have shown, and are asking us to do what was done for them during the time Of the so-called and mis-called national policy, which I hope this government will never consent to. I should be proud as u Canadian to know that the label ' made in Canada ' was a guarantee of a good article. But I am ashamed, as a Canadian, that it is not so. And, if Canadian goods are not of good enough quality to sell in Canada in competition with outside manufactured goods, how are we to expect our Canadian trade in manufactured articles with the outside world to increase ? We are to put up the duties on manufactured articles and squeeze the limit out of $174,000,000 worth of trade of our mines, fisheries, animals and agriculture. And for what ? Will it increase by one cent the wages of the operatives in the mills and factories 7 It never did before. No; the object is to increase the dividends of the capitalists engaged in these industries- capital which is so fully represented in this House and so strongly represented on the other side particularly.
It seems, there has been a special attack made upon the government by our friends who are in the woollen industry. The woollen industry it appears, is hard hit by the British preference, and it cannot survive

I am giving it credit for honesty. It is hard hit and cannot survive, if the preference is continued. Our woollen mills are being shut up, and the operatives thrown out of employment and compelled to seek employment in the United States. We are called upon to give adequate protection to the woollen industry. I took the trouble to look up the customs tariff and to make some little inquiry with regard to this woollen industry, and I would like to know what the woollen manufacturers want. Remember that Canada is a country with a long winter. Canada is a country where cheap woollens is of the highest importance to the people. Where a very trifling difference in the cost means a tremendous tax, particularly upon the labouring and poorer classes of this country. Woollen goods are a prime necessity, an absolute necessity, a universal necessity. Lower the cost of woollens and you benefit everybody, aud particularly you benefit these great producing industries that I have mentioned. Increase the cost of woollens, and you injure everybody, and you especially injure these great producing industries that I have mentioned. You injure the labouring people; the poorer classes above all others. I say that when men come to this House and demand an increase in the duties 53
on woollens, it is for them to show good cause why those duties should be increased.
Now, what are the duties on woollens today ? In the customs tariff there is a duty in favour of the woollen manufacturers, if I read it right, of 35 per cent; 35 per cent against the world, 35 per cent against the danger of this country being used as a slaughter market by the woollen manufactures of the United States, a danger which, I may say, does not exist, as woollens are much dearer in the United States than they are in Canada. However, we have a tariff of 35 per cent in favour of woollens against the world, and with the British preference taken off we have a duty of 23 per cent against Great Britain, on woollen manufactures at large. I find that where other articles are required to enter into the manufactures of wool, such as alpaca, camel's wool, &c., these are admitted free for the benefit of our friends the woollen manufacturers-very properly so, too, I think. I do not know how many of our woollen manufacturers make shoddy, I hope none of them do. But 1-notice that probably in response to their request woollen rags were put on the free list. So they get a considerable part of their raw material free; they get protection of more than one-third against the world, and 23 per cent against Great Britain, 3 per cent more than the manufacturers of agricultural implements get to-day, 3 per cent more than the horse-raisers of the North-west, or of Canada generally get to-day, 3 per cent more, I may mention, than the raw wool, the product of the farm, receives to-day. That is to say, raw wool gets a protection of 3 cents a pound, and giving an estimated price of 15 cents a pound for wool, that leaves 20 per cent in favour of the farmer, while the manufacturer gets 23 per cent under the preferential tariff. I notice also that woollen yarn is protected to the extent of 30 per cent, while yarn which comes in for the purpose of manufacture pays only 20 per cent.
Now, I ask in all conscience, if these woollen manufacturers are not satisfied at present, what do they want ? They are protected against the slaughter market of the United States by more than one-third of the cost of the imported article; they have cheap food, cheaper than it is in Great Britain; they have water power such as does not exist in Great Britain; they have capital in this country ample for all needs; they have protection more than many other industries have. Now, what more do they want ? Do they want these great producing industries of the mine, the forest, the sea and the farm, to pay such extra price on the goods which they manufacture as will enable them to carry on their business by antiquated methods and antiquated means ? If their demand means anything it means that, and I am here to say that in my humble estimation that demand should be refused in the interest of the-whole of the people of this country. .



1 will carry the argument further. I am quite aware that you cannot eat your cake and have it. I want to be understood as saying that if this woollen manufacturing industry cannot exist in Canada under all the favourable conditions which it has at present, better that it should pass out of existence, that the capital employed in It should find other fields of employment, that the labour employed in it should find other fields, than that the people of this country at large should have to pay an unreasonable amount for one of the greatest necessities of their lives, and particularly that the poorer classes should be taxed unduly for the benefit of a few capitalists. I do not think that any such conclusion is in prospect, I do not think that we stand in any such danger. But I certainly say that if the choice has to be made, let these gentlemen understand distinctly that there are men in this House pre-pard to make it. They themselves are to be the judges. When we in the Northwest find that a certain article of our production cannot find a market, we are told to change our production, and we do. We have to; and if we do not, I do not know any tariff on earth that would save us. We did not find that our friends, the opposition, when they were in power, ever took the trouble to try to shape the tariff so as to save us when we were badly off in regard to markets. Neither have they a right to demand that we should do unreasonable things simply because they are incompetent in the management of their own business.
I notice that one of our friends alluded to protection on buggies. He claimed that the buggy industry was in danger of serious damage because of a lack of protection. I find that buggies have per cent protection. That if you buy a buggy in the United States and bring it over to Canada, you have to pay one-third of the original cost to our hon. friend the Minister of Customs, before you can bring that buggy in. Now, if that is not a sufficient protection to Canadian buggy manufacturers, X want to know what they desire. For I find that the wood, even, though in a partly manufactured state, that is required for the making of that buggy, is allowed to come in free. I heard one of our friends speak on the subject of cutlery, our cutlery trade was going to be ruined. I find that cutlery has a protection of 30 per cent, very nearly one-third. I find further that if our friends the manufacturers of cutlery only desire to do a finishing business and do not really desire to go into the business of actually manufacturing the article which they sell as of Canadian make, they have the privilege of importing those parts of cutlery which go to make up the finished article, under a duty of 10 per cent.
I won't trouble the House by going through the whole tariff list But I will

say that my study of the present tariff has led me to the belief that it has been a subject of more careful adjustment than 1 ever thought it was, and that there has been more done to relieve the tax on the consumer and at the same time help the manufacturer-which we all wish to do- than a careless glance at the tariff pages would give anybody to understand. In regard to the reductions in duties that have taken place, and in regard to the effect of these reductions it has been said that the reductions only amounted to such and sucli a per cent. I do not know whether that calculation is correct or not, and I do not care, but I do know that the reductions of the protective duties on iron and steel, which had done no good to this country and had simply been a tax upon it, were' a benefit to our manufacturers which they certainly availed themselves of and which we are all very glad of. There was, an advantage, a distinct advantage to the country In the readjustment of these iron duties, the story of which is not told by the mere amount of the reduction.
I am no enemy of the manufacturers. I am anxious to see the manufacturing interests of this country prosper, as I am anxious to see every other industry prosper, but, I cannot agree to a declaration of policy whereby that industry is to be singled out to be benefited at the expense of all others. You say that it is not, in terms. Well, it does not need to be in terms. There is a difference between an industry which is chiefly an exporting industry and an industry which chiefly finds a home market. The one is capable of being affected by a protective tariff, and the other is not correspondingly capable of being affected by a protective tariff. If , you put a duty on woollen goods, you enable the price of woollen goods to be raised, but if you put a duty on wheat you do not raise the price of the wheat of the farmer as long as he has to export the millions and millions of bushels that he raises. I was struck by the argument of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) where he said that the population of Canada consumes 22,000,000 bushels of wheat a year, and that it should be possible to ensure a home market to our people to that extent. Possibly it would, but what about the balance of the crop ? What is he going to do about that ? Is he going to protect the farmer on 20,000,000 bushels of his crop, enable the farmer to bleed every other industry in the country and still compel him to sell the balance of his product in the world's market at the world's price ? That is the best he can do for the farmer, but it is not the best he can do for the woollen manufacturer who makes only for the home market. Every cent which is added to the duty is a cent in the pocket of the capitalist who owns the woollen mill. That is

the difference between protection as applied to the manufacturers and protection as applied to a great producing industry.
I said that I was a protectionist Mr. Speaker, I am a protectionist. I believe in the policy of protection. I believe it is the first business of a government to do what lies in its power by legislation, administration or otherwise to protect and advance the interest of the people of the country of which it has charge. I want to see a protectionist policy on behalf of labour in this country. I want to see a policy that will protect labour against the degradation of unfair competition. We have heard a great deal on the subject of Chinese labour in British Columbia. Let me say that if there are 16,000 adult working Chinamen in British Columbia that displaces, possibly, not 16,000, but, certainly
8,000	adult white labourers, taking one white man to be as good as two Chinamen. Sixteen thousand Chinamen displace 8,000 white men, but, the 8,000 white men would probably lie 8,000 heads of families and would mean not 8,000 people, but 40,000 people in that province-40,000 added to the strength of our nation; instead of 16,000 towards the weakness of our nation. For the labour of the country is the vitality of the country. It is on the strength and force of the labour of the world that the industrial machine depends just as much as it is on the pressure of steam in the boiler that we depend for the running of our machinery. If we have plenty of the right kind of people we can do business, and if we have not, we cannot. If we allow the right kind of people to be displaced by the wrong kind of people we do ourselves an injury. I say that I am in favour of a policy of protection to labour, protecting labour from the degradation of low wages and unfair competition in so far as that can be done. It is all a mistake for us to consider that it is merely the capitalist and his capital that has to be considered in the successful running of the affairs of the country.
The foundation of everything is the labourer and his labour and any system of taxation which takes an unfair proportion of the public revenue from the labourer is an injury to the country as much as it is to the labourers themselves. Last night, or the night before, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) asked :	How is it
that there is only one free trade country in the world, that all the other countries of Europe and America are protectionist V How can it be that these are all wrong and that Great Britain alone is right ? On the other hand, let me ask him in what other country has there been, under paralleled circumstances, any such industrial or commercial development as there has been in Great Britain under the system which has prevailed there. There is no comparison between the progress of Great Bri-
53 i
tain and the progress of any other country, and the one thing in which Great Britain is placed above any other protective country is that the British workingman is the man who pays the least taxes of any one in the British islands. He is the man, who by the British system is relieved of taxation practically, and there you have the secret of Britain's 'industrial supremacy so far as that supremacy has been achieved, and so far as it has been maintained. I say that in this country, our system of tariff and our system of taxation ought above all things be framed so as to lay the least burden upon the labouring man and upon the results of his labour to himself and his family.
I am a protectionist in this : That I wish to see our country grow, and grow great I submit that there is nothing in which our country has lost so much, and has fallen so far short of achieving greatness, as in the stupendous loss of population which has taken place within the last thirty years. During that period Canada has lost over a million of her native born children. Canada has been losing them decade after decade, and if she is not losing them to-day then we have reason to be pleased. But we have more than reason to fear that she is still losing them in larger numbers than is good for the country. I am in favour of a policy which will actively endeavour to retain our own population in our own country for its advancement and its building up. I heard my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) say that he was in favour of that idea, and he proposed to attain it by providing protection to manufacturing industries. Well, my hon. friend's friends were in power for nearly twenty years. They had a policy which they called the national policy and one of the great purposes of that policy was to do that very thing. They had time enough to work it out to a successful conclusion if success was possible under it. The result of the census has shown that success was not achieved, and therefore I believe that success under that policy was not possible. It is impossible to herd the surplus people of this country in manufacturing centres, which manufacturing centres depend on the balance of the people for their support and their prosperity. The thing is an impossibility. Let me place this fact before hon. gentlemen: Canada offers to-day the greatest field for the employment of intelligent labour that is offered by any country in the world. Canada has opportunity for every one of her children and will have such an opportunity for decades and decades to come. That opportunity lies in the country west of Lake Superior-in Manitoba, in British Columbia, in the North-west Territories and in the Yukon. It is by attracting the overflow of the people of our eastern provinces to our western provinces that we will retain their nationality and retain their labour

and their enterprise for the benefit of our own country. That is the way in which we can do it, and that is the only way in which we can do it. You may say : Why is it not being done ; why has it not been done; or perhaps you may say : Is it not being done. Well, I am sorry to say Mr. Speaker, that it is not being done, that it has not been done, and that it has been the declared policy of the government of Canada for many years-the declared policy of the present government and of the preceding government-not to use means to induce the removal of population from one part of the Dominion to the other. I stand here to-night to say that that declared policy has been the greatest curse from which our Dominion has suffered; that that policy of knowing nothing and doing nothing in regard to the removal of our population from one part of the country where they had not opportunity to the other part of the country where they had boundless opportunity, has been the reason why so many of our people have gone to that other country where they had opportunity as well. In view of the census returns, in view of the facts which are now before us, I say that it is time for our country to drop its know nothing and do nothing policy in regard to retaining our own people for our own country, and to recognize the fact that of all the countries in the known world, this Canada of ours is the country which sends out the greatest proportion of its people as emigrants to other countries. If we realize that, and if we realize as I believe-and as I think we all believe-that our own people are the best people we can have for the settlement and development of our country ; surely here is a policy that is worthy of the best attention of our best minds and the best efforts that our government can puf forth. There is only one means by which the exodus can be checked, can be stopped, and that is by turning our overflow of population into the field which we acquired for that very purpose thirty or forty years ago. If we did not acquire the North-west for that purpose we did not acquire it for any reasonable purpose ; because, if you settle that country with an alien people it has such a preponderance of resources and of opportunities that the question presents itself : What becomes of your Dominion ; what becomes of the country that you are supposed to be building up ? How long can you hold it as a part of this Dominion when that country is filled with an alien people and outnumbers the population of Eastern Canada by ten or twenty to one. It is of the first necessity towards the building up of a Canadian nation that you must use every endeavour to put every son of Canadian soil into that western country where, and where only within your borders there is room and opportunity suited to his intellect and ability.
